content: 1. The resolution of hepatitis C was discussed in the Journal of Virology in 2004, specifically in volume 78, pages 5867-5874. 2. Guidelines for the screening, care, and treatment of individuals with hepatitis C infection were published in a document accessed on March 29, 2022. 3. Updated guidelines for the screening, care, and treatment of individuals with chronic hepatitis C infection were released by the World Health Organization in April 2016. This document is available online and was accessed on March 29, 2022. 4. A comprehensive review of hepatitis C diagnostic technologies was published in a document accessed on March 29, 2022. 5. Tanaka et al. (1996) studied serum levels of hepatitis C virus core protein in patients with chronic hepatitis C treated with interferon alfa, as published in Hepatology, volume 23, pages 1330-1333. 6. Tillmann HL (2014) explored the role of hepatitis C virus core antigen testing in diagnosis, disease monitoring, and treatment in the World Journal of Gastroenterology, volume 20, pages 6701-6706. 7. The London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine team, including Boerass, Amini, Falconer, Kelly, and Peeling, contributed to hepatitis C research in 2015. 8. The WHO Prequalification of In Vitro Diagnostics program released a public report on the Xpert HCV Viral Load assay, compatible with GeneXpert Dx, GeneXpert Infinity-48s, and GeneXpert Infinity-80 systems. This report was accessed on March 30, 2022. 9. Another WHO Prequalification report detailed the Genedrive HCV ID Kit, with public documentation available under PQDx 0380-133-00. 10. WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis, specifically Module 2 on systematic screening for tuberculosis disease, were accessed on March 29, 2022. 11. The WHO Global Health Impact Group Team conducted a systematic review on the clinical impact of point-of-care early infant diagnosis for HIV, published in 2020. 12. Le Roux et al. (2020) performed a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing the clinical and operational impact of point-of-care versus laboratory-based nucleic acid testing for routine HIV viral load monitoring. 13. WHO consolidated guidelines on tuberculosis diagnosis, specifically Module 3 on rapid diagnostics for tuberculosis detection, were accessed on March 29, 2022. 14. Mohamed et al. (2020) demonstrated that point-of-care screening and streamlined linkage to care significantly improved hepatitis C treatment uptake among prisoners in England, as published in the International Journal of Drug Policy, volume 75, article 102608. 15. Mohamed et al. (2020) also evaluated the cost-effectiveness of strategies to enhance HCV screening, linkage-to-care, and treatment in remand prison settings in England, as published in Liver International, volume 40, pages 2950-2960. 16. Duchesne et al. (2020) estimated the cost-effectiveness of testing strategies for diagnosing hepatitis C virus infection in Central and Western Africa using a model-based approach, as published in PLoS One, volume 15, article e0238035. 17. Duchesne et al. (2020) also assessed the cost-effectiveness of testing strategies for diagnosing HCV infection among people who inject drugs in Senegal, as published in the International Journal of Drug Policy, volume 75, article 102613. 18. Freiman et al. (2016) conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis on hepatitis C core antigen testing for diagnosing HCV infection, as published in Annals of Internal Medicine, volume 165, pages 345-355. 19. Vermehren et al. (2008) evaluated RNA detection and quantification methods for hepatitis C virus in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology, volume 46, pages 3880-3891. 20. Sabato et al. (2007) compared the performance characteristics of three real-time reverse transcription-PCR test systems for detecting and quantifying hepatitis C virus, as published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology, volume 45, pages 2529-2536. 21. Yu et al. (2000) studied qualitative and quantitative AMPLICOR reverse transcription-PCR tests for hepatitis C virus RNA, focusing on calibration to international units, enhanced genotype reactivity, and performance characteristics, as published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology, volume 38, pages 4171-4179. 22. Freiman et al. (2019) analyzed a global dataset to derive the optimal limit of detection for an HCV point-of-care test for viremic infection, as published in the Journal of Hepatology, volume 71, pages 62-70. 23. Harrington et al. (2019) examined HCV RNA levels following virologic failure with direct-acting antivirals and its implications for lower sensitivity diagnostic assays, as published in Clinical Infectious Diseases, volume 70, pages 327-330. 24. Moscato et al. (2011) investigated the quantitative determination of hepatitis C core antigen in therapy monitoring for chronic hepatitis C, as published in Intervirology, volume 54, pages 61-65. 25. Feng et al. (2014) identified hepatitis C virus core antigen as an earlier and stronger predictor of sustained virological response in patients with genotype 1 HCV infection, as published in BMC Gastroenterology, volume 14, article 47. 26. Takahashi et al. (2005) highlighted the benefit of HCV core antigen assay in predicting therapeutic response to interferon and ribavirin combination therapy, as published in 2005, volume 43, pages 186-191. 27. Fujino et al. (2009) demonstrated that early decline of HCV core antigen can predict sustained virological response in patients treated with pegylated interferon plus ribavirin combination therapy, as published in the Journal of Digestive Diseases, volume 10, pages 21-25. 28. Loggi et al. (2013) analyzed patterns of HCV-RNA and HCV core antigen in early monitoring of standard treatment for chronic hepatitis C, as published in the Journal of Clinical Virology, volume 56, pages 207-211. 29. Okazaki et al. (2008) evaluated a high-range method for early detection of hepatitis C virus infection, as published in Rinsho Byori, volume 56, pages 95-100. 30. Schnuriger et al. (2006) assessed a new combined antigen-antibody detection assay for early detection of HCV infection, particularly in HIV co-infected individuals, as published in Pathologie Biologie (Paris), volume 54, pages 578-586. 31. Van Helden and Weiskirchen (2014) clinically evaluated HCV-core antigen determination for hepatitis C diagnostics, as published in Zeitschrift für Gastroenterologie, volume 52, pages 1164-1170. 32. Gu et al. (2014) compared the performance of HCV antigen and RNA kits for screening HCV-infected samples, as published in the Chinese Journal of Biologicals, volume 27, pages 1181-1184. 33. Mohamed et al. (2020) conducted an in-field evaluation of the Xpert HCV Viral Load Fingerstick assay among people who inject drugs in Tanzania, as published in Liver International, volume 40, pages 514-521. 34. Chevaliez et al. (2020) assessed molecular point-of-care testing and dried blood spot methods for HCV screening in people who inject drugs, as published in Open Forum Infectious Diseases, volume 7. 35. Patel et al. (2016) reviewed the performance of HCV Ag or RNA kits for screening HCV-infected samples, as published in Public Health Reports, volume 131, supplement 2, pages 12-19. 36. Janjua et al. (2016) analyzed the population-level cascade of care for hepatitis C in British Columbia, Canada, as part of the BC Hepatitis Testers Cohort (BC-HTC), as published in EBioMedicine, volume 12, pages 189-195. 37. Mera et al. (2016) reported on the identification and clinical management of individuals with chronic HCV infection in the Cherokee Nation from 2012 to 2015, as published in MMWR Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, volume 65, pages 461-466. 38. Madden et al. (2018) explored residual barriers to direct-acting antiviral hepatitis C treatment for people who inject drugs, beyond interferon side effects, as published in PLoS One, volume 13, article e0207226. 39. Ireland et al. (2019) assessed the uptake, impact, and costs of hepatitis C reflex testing and its implications for policy. 40. Ireland et al. (2019) also evaluated the adoption of reflex RNA testing on hepatitis C antibody-positive samples. 41. López-Martínez et al. (2019) demonstrated significant improvement in HCV diagnosis using a one-step strategy in a central laboratory, as published in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology, volume 58. 42. Bartlett et al. (2019) analyzed the population-level care cascade for hepatitis C in British Columbia, Canada, as of 2018, focusing on the impact of direct-acting antivirals, as published in Liver International, volume 39, pages 2261-2272. 43. The National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence (2012) provided guidance on promoting and offering hepatitis B and C testing to individuals at increased risk of infection. 44. Public Health England (2017) released a report on screening for hepatitis C infection. 45. The Royal College of Pathologists and the Institute of Biomedical Science (2015) issued guidance on the retention and storage of pathological records and specimens.
